entries.b3f31341aea40e08a6cae8b5ebc086f1a77dce52: <div sID="gen4123" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Josh.3" sID="Josh.3"/> <div eID="gen4123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4124" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4125" type="x-p"/> This chapter, and that which follows it, give us the history of Israel's passing through Jordan into Canaan, and a very memorable history it is. Long afterwards, they are told to remember what God did for them between Shittim (whence they decamped, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.1">ver. 1</reference>) and Gilgal, where they next pitched, <reference osisRef="Josh.4.19">ch. iv. 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.5">Mic. vi. 5</reference>, that they might know the righteousness of the Lord. By Joshua's order they marched up to the river's side, (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.1">ver. 1</reference>), and then almighty power led them through it. They passed through the Red Sea unexpectedly, and in their flight by night, but they have notice some time before of their passing through Jordan, and their expectations raised. I. The people are directed to follow the ark, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.2-Josh.3.4">ver. 2-4</reference>. II. They are commanded to sanctify themselves, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.5">ver. 5</reference>. III. The priests with the ark are ordered to lead the van, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.6">ver. 6</reference>. IV. Joshua is magnified and made commander in chief, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.7-Josh.3.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. V. Public notice is given of what God is about to do for them, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.9-Josh.3.13">ver. 9-13</reference>. IV. The thing is done, Jordan is divided, and Israel brought safely through it, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.14-Josh.3.17">ver. 14-17</reference>. This was the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes.
entries.443fd53086800d6ce36caf4b86e37f94f9826329: <div eID="gen4125" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4124" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Preparation for Passing over the Jordan. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen4126" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Joshua rose early in the morning; and they removed from Shittim, and came to Jordan, he and all the children of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it came to pass after three days, that the officers went through the host; <hi type="super">3</hi> And they commanded the people, saying, When ye see the ark of the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, and the priests the Levites bearing it, then ye shall remove from your place, and go after it. <hi type="super">4</hi> Yet there shall be a space between you and it, about two thousand cubits by measure: come not near unto it, that ye may know the way by which ye must go: for ye have not passed <hi type="italic">this</hi> way heretofore. <hi type="super">5</hi> And Joshua said unto the people, Sanctify yourselves: for to morrow the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will do wonders among you. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Joshua spake unto the priests, saying, Take up the ark of the covenant, and pass over before the people. And they took up the ark of the covenant, and went before the people. <div eID="gen4126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4127" type="x-p"/> Rahab, in mentioning to the spies the <hi type="italic">drying up of the Red Sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.2.10">ch. ii. 10</reference>), the report of which terrified the Canaanites more than anything else, intimates that those on that side the water expected that Jordan, that great defence of their country, would in like manner give way to them. Whether the Israelites had any expectation of it does not appear. God often <hi type="italic">did things for them which they looked not for,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.64.3">Isa. lxiv. 3</reference>. Now here we are told, <div eID="gen4127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4128" type="x-p"/> I. That they <hi type="italic">came to Jordan and lodged there,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.3.1">v. 1</reference>. Though they were not yet told how they should pass the river, and were unprovided for the passing of it in any ordinary way, yet they went forward in faith, having been told (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.11">ch. i. 11</reference>) that they should pass it. We must go on in the way of our duty though we foresee difficulties, trusting God to help us through them when we come to them. Let us proceed as far as we can, and depend on divine sufficiency for that which we find ourselves not sufficient for. In this march Joshua led them, and particular notice is taken of his early rising as there is afterwards upon other occasions (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.12">ch. vi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.7.16">vii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.8.10">viii. 10</reference>), which intimates how little he loved his ease, how much he loved his business, and what care and pains he was willing to take in it. Those that would bring great things to pass must rise early. <hi type="italic">Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty.</hi> Joshua herein set a good example to the officers under him, and taught them to rise early, and to all that are in public stations especially to attend continually to the duty of their place. <div eID="gen4128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4129" type="x-p"/> II. That the people were directed to follow the ark. Officers were appointed to go through the host to give these directions (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.2">v. 2</reference>), that every Israelite might know both what to do and what to depend upon. <div eID="gen4129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4130" type="x-p"/> 1. They might depend upon the ark to lead them; that is, upon God himself, of whose presence the ark was an instituted sign and token. It seems, the pillar of cloud and fire was removed, else that would have led them, unless we suppose that it now hovered over the ark and so they had a double guide: honour was put upon the ark, and a defence upon that glory. It is called here the <hi type="italic">ark of the covenant of the Lord their God.</hi> What greater encouragement could they have than this, that the Lord was their God, a God in covenant with them? Here was the <hi type="italic">ark of the covenant;</hi> if God be ours, we need not fear any evil. He was nigh to them, present with them, went before them: what could come amiss to those that were thus guided, thus guarded? Formerly the ark was carried in the midst of the camp, but now it went before them to <hi type="italic">search out a resting-place</hi> for them (<reference osisRef="Num.10.33">Num. x. 33</reference>), and, as it were, to give them livery and seisin of the promised land, and put them in possession of it. In the ark the tables of the law were, and over it the mercy-seat; for the divine law and grace reigning in the heart are the surest pledges of God's presence and favour, and those that would be led to the heavenly Canaan must take the law of God for their guide (<hi type="italic">if thou wilt enter into life keep the commandments</hi>) and have the great propitiation in their eye, <hi type="italic">looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.</hi> <div eID="gen4130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4131" type="x-p"/> 2. They might depend upon the priests and Levites, who were appointed for that purpose to carry the ark before them. The work of ministers is to hold forth the word of life, and to take care of the administration of those ordinances which are the tokens of God's presence and the instruments of his power and grace; and herein they must go before the people of God in their way to heaven. <div eID="gen4131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4132" type="x-p"/> 3. The people must follow the ark: <hi type="italic">Remove from your place and go after it,</hi> (1.) As those that are resolved never to forsake it. Wherever God's ordinances are, there we must be; if they flit, we must remove and go after them. (2.) As those that are entirely satisfied in its guidance, that it will lead in the best way to the best end; and therefore, <hi type="italic">Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest.</hi> This must be all their care, to attend the motions of the ark, and follow it with an implicit faith. Thus must we walk after the rule of the word and the direction of the Spirit in every thing, so shall <hi type="italic">peace be upon us,</hi> as it now was upon the Israel of God. They must follow the priests as far as they carried the ark, but no further; so we must follow our ministers only as they follow Christ. <div eID="gen4132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4133" type="x-p"/> 4. In following the ark, they must <hi type="italic">keep their distance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.3.4">v. 4</reference>. They must none of them come within a thousand yards of the ark. (1.) They must thus express their awful and reverent regard to that token of God's presence, lest its familiarity with them should breed contempt. This charge to them not to come near was agreeable to that dispensation of darkness, bondage, and terror: but we now through Christ have access with boldness. (2.) Thus it was made to appear that the ark was able to protect itself, and needed not to be guarded by the men of war, but was itself a guard to them. With what a noble defiance of the enemy did it leave all it its friends half a mile behind except the unarmed priests that carried it as perfectly sufficient for its own safety and theirs that followed it! (3.) Thus it was the better seen by those that were to be led by it: <hi type="italic">That you may know the way by which you must go,</hi> seeing it, as it were, chalked out or tracked by the ark. Had they been allowed to come near it, they would have surrounded it, and none would have had the sight of it but those that were close to it; but, as it was put at such a distance before them, they would all have the satisfaction of seeing it, and would be animated by the sight. And it was with good reason that this provision was made for their encouragement: <hi type="italic">For you have not passed this way heretofore.</hi> This had been the character of all their way through the wilderness, it was an untrodden path, but this especially through Jordan. While we are here we must expect and prepare for unusual events, to pass ways that we have not passed before, and much more when we go hence; our way through the <hi type="italic">valley of the shadow of death</hi> is a way we have not gone before, which makes it the more formidable. But, if we have the assurance of God's presence, we need not fear; that will furnish us with such strength as we never had when we come to do a work we never did. <div eID="gen4133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4134" type="x-p"/> III. They were commanded to sanctify themselves, that they might be prepared to attend the ark; and with good reason: For <hi type="italic">to-morrow the Lord will do wonders among you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.3.5">v. 5</reference>. See how magnificently he speaks of God's works: he <hi type="italic">doeth wonders,</hi> and is therefore to be adored, admired, and trusted in. See how intimately acquainted Joshua was with the divine counsels: he could tell before-hand what god would do, and when. See what preparation we must make to receive the discoveries of God's glory and the communications of his grace: we must sanctify ourselves. This we must do when we are to attend the ark, and God by it is about to do wonders among us; we must separate ourselves from all other cares, devote ourselves to God's honour, and <hi type="italic">cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit.</hi> The people of Israel were now entering into the holy land, and therefore must sanctify themselves. God was about to give them uncommon instances of his favour, which by meditation and prayer they must compose their minds to a very careful observation of, that they might give God the glory, and take to themselves the comfort, of these appearances. <div eID="gen4134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4135" type="x-p"/> IV. The priests were ordered to take up the ark and carry it <hi type="italic">before the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.3.6">v. 6</reference>. It was the Levites' work ordinarily to carry the ark, <reference osisRef="Num.4.15">Num. iv. 15</reference>. But on this great occasion the priests were ordered to do it. And they did as they were commanded, <hi type="italic">took up the ark,</hi> and did not think themselves disparaged, <hi type="italic">went before the people,</hi> and did not think themselves exposed; the ark they carried was both their honour and their defence. And now we may suppose that prayer of Moses used, when the ark set forward (<reference osisRef="Num.10.35">Num. x. 35</reference>), <hi type="italic">Rise up, Lord and let they enemies be scattered.</hi> Magistrates are here instructed to stir up ministers to their work, and to make use of their authority for the furtherance of religion. Ministers must likewise learn to go before in the way of God, and not to shrink nor draw back when dangers are before them. They must expect to be most struck at, but they <hi type="italic">know whom they have trusted.</hi>
entries.8a9963c8dbe1bed01589b9b9c3fa8ebacd02a1b7: <div eID="gen4135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4136" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Joshua, This day will I begin to magnify thee in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, <hi type="italic">so</hi> I will be with thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> And thou shalt command the priests that bear the ark of the covenant, saying, When ye are come to the brink of the water of Jordan, ye shall stand still in Jordan. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Joshua said unto the children of Israel, Come hither, and hear the words of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Joshua said, Hereby ye shall know that the living God <hi type="italic">is</hi> among you, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Hivites, and the Perizzites, and the Girgashites, and the Amorites, and the Jebusites. <hi type="super">11</hi> Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth passeth over before you into Jordan. <hi type="super">12</hi> Now therefore take you twelve men out of the tribes of Israel, out of every tribe a man. <hi type="super">13</hi> And it shall come to pass, as soon as the soles of the feet of the priests that bear the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of Jordan, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the waters of Jordan shall be cut off <hi type="italic">from</hi> the waters that come down from above; and they shall stand upon a heap. <div eID="gen4136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4137" type="x-p"/> We may observe here how God honours Joshua, and by this wondrous work he is about to do designs to make Israel know that he is their governor, and then how Joshua honours God and endeavours by it to make Israel know that he is their God. Thus those that honour God he will honour, and those whom he has advanced should do what they can in their places to exalt him. <div eID="gen4137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4138" type="x-p"/> I. God speaks to Joshua to put honour upon him, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.7-Josh.3.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. 1. It was a great honour God did him that he spoke to him as he had done to Moses from off the mercy-seat, before the priests removed it with the ark. This would make Joshua easy in himself and great among the people, that God was pleased to speak so familiarly to him. 2. That he designed to <hi type="italic">magnify him in the sight of all Israel.</hi> He had told him before that he would be with him (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.5">ch. i. 5</reference>), and that comforted him, but now all Israel shall see it, and this would magnify him. Those are truly great with whom God is and whom he employs and owns in his service. God magnified him because he would have the people magnify him. Pious magistrates are to be highly honoured and esteemed as public blessings, and the more we see of God with them the more we should honour them. By the dividing of the Red Sea Israel was convinced that God was with Moses in bringing them out of Egypt; therefore they are said to be <hi type="italic">baptized unto Moses in the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.2">1 Cor. x. 2</reference>. And upon that occasion they <hi type="italic">believed him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.14.31">Exod. xiv. 31</reference>. And now, by the dividing of Jordan, they shall be convinced that God is in like manner with Joshua in bringing them into Canaan. God had magnified Joshua before on several occasions, but now he began to magnify him as the successor of Moses in the government. Some have observed that it was at the banks of Jordan that God began to magnify Joshua, and at the same place he began to magnify our Lord Jesus as Mediator; for John was baptizing at Bethabara, <hi type="italic">the house of passage,</hi> and there it was that when our Saviour was baptized it was proclaimed concerning him, <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son.</hi> 3. That by him he gave orders to the priests themselves, though they were his immediate attendants (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt command the priests,</hi> that is, "Thou shalt make known to them the divine command in this matter, and take care that they observe it, to stand still at the brink of Jordan while the waters part, that it may appear to be <hi type="italic">at the presence of the Lord,</hi> of the mighty God of Jacob, that Jordan is <hi type="italic">driven back,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.114.5">Ps. cxiv. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.7">7</reference>. God could have divided the river without the priests, but they could not without him. The priests must herein set a good example to the people, and teach them to do their utmost in the service of God, and trust him for help in time of need. <div eID="gen4138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4139" type="x-p"/> II. Joshua speaks to the people, and therein honours God. <div eID="gen4139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4140" type="x-p"/> 1. He demands attention (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Come hither</hi> to me, as many as can come within hearing, and, before you see the works, <hi type="italic">hear the words of the Lord your God,</hi> that you may compare them together and they may illustrate each other." He had commanded them to sanctify themselves, and therefore calls them to <hi type="italic">hear the word of God,</hi> for that is the ordinary means of sanctification, <reference osisRef="John.17.17">John xvii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen4140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4141" type="x-p"/> 2. He now tells them, at length, by what way they should pass over Jordan, by the stopping of its streams (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">The waters of Jordan shall be cut off.</hi> God could by a sudden and miraculous frost have congealed the surface, so that they might all have gone over upon the ice; but that being a thing sometimes done even in that country by the ordinary power of nature (<reference osisRef="Job.38.30">Job xxxviii. 30</reference>), it would not have been such an honour to Israel's God, nor such a terror to Israel's enemies; it must therefore be done in such a way as had no precedent but the dividing of the Red Sea: and that miracle is here repeated, to show that God has the same power to finish the salvation of his people that he had to begin it, for he is the <hi type="italic">Alpha</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Omega;</hi> and that <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord</hi> (as the Chaldee reads it, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.7">v. 7</reference>), the essential, eternal Word, was as truly with Joshua as he was with Moses. And by the dividing of the waters from the waters, and the making of the dry land to appear which had been covered, God would remind them of that in which Moses by revelation had instructed them concerning the work of creation (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.6">Gen. i. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.9">9</reference>), that by what they now saw their belief of that which they there read might be assisted, and they might know that the God whom they worshipped was the same God that made the world and that it was the same power that was engaged and employed for them. <div eID="gen4141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4142" type="x-p"/> 3. The people having been directed before to follow the ark are here told that it should <hi type="italic">pass before them into Jordan,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.3.11">v. 11</reference>. Observe, (1.) The ark of the covenant must be their guide. During the reign of Moses, the cloud was their guide, but now, in Joshua's reign, the ark; both were visible signs of God's presence and presidency, but divine grace under the Mosaic dispensation was wrapt up as in a cloud and covered with a veil, while by Christ, our Joshua, it is revealed in the ark of the covenant unveiled. (2.) It is called <hi type="italic">the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth.</hi> "He that is your God (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.9">v. 9</reference>), in covenant with you, is the <hi type="italic">Lord of all the earth,</hi> has both right and power to command, control, use, and dispose of all nations and of all creatures. He is the <hi type="italic">Lord of all the earth,</hi> therefore he needs not you, nor can he be benefited by you; therefore it is your honour and happiness to have him in covenant with you: if he be yours, all the creatures are at your service, and when he pleases shall be employed for you." When we are praising and worshipping God as Israel's God, and ours through Christ, we must remember that he is the <hi type="italic">Lord of the whole earth,</hi> and reverence him and trust in him accordingly. Some observe an accent in the original, which they think directs us to translate it somewhat more emphatically, <hi type="italic">Behold the ark of the covenant, even the ark of the Lord, or even of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth.</hi> (3.) They are told that the ark should <hi type="italic">pass before them into Jordan.</hi> God would not appoint them to go any where but where he himself would go before them and go with them; and they might safely venture, even into Jordan itself, if the ark of the covenant led them. While we make God's precepts our rule, his promises our stay, and his providence our guide, we need not dread the greatest difficulties we may meet with in the way of duty. That promise is sure to all the seed (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.2">Isa. xliii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">When thou passes through the waters I will be with thee, and through the rivers they shall not overflow thee.</hi> <div eID="gen4142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4143" type="x-p"/> 4. From what God was now about to do for them he infers an assurance of what he would yet further do. This he mentions first, so much was his heart upon it, and so great a satisfaction did it give him (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hereby you shall know that the living God</hi> (the true God, and God of power, not one of the dead gods of the heathen) <hi type="italic">is among you,</hi> though you see him not, nor are to have any image of him, is among you to give you law, secure your welfare, and receive your homage,—is among you in this great undertaking now before you; and therefore you shall, nay, he himself <hi type="italic">will, without fail, drive out from before you the Canaanites.</hi>" So that the dividing of Jordan was intended to be to them, (1.) A sure token of God's presence with them. By this they could not but <hi type="italic">know that God was among them,</hi> unless their unbelief was as obstinate against the most convincing evidence as that of their fathers was, who presently after God had divided the Red Sea before them, impudently asked, <hi type="italic">Is the Lord among us, or is he not?</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.17.7">Exod. xvii. 7</reference>. (2.) A sure pledge of the conquest of Canaan. "If the living God is among you, <hi type="italic">expelling he will expel</hi> (so the Hebrew phrase is) <hi type="italic">from before you the Canaanites.</hi>" He will do it certainly, and do it effectually. What should hinder him? What can stand in his way before whom rivers are divided and dried up? The forcing of the lines was certain presage of the ruin of all their hosts: how could they stand their ground when Jordan itself was driven back? When they had not courage to dispute this pass, but trembled at the approach of the <hi type="italic">mighty God of Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.7">Ps. cxiv. 7</reference>), what opposition could they ever make after this? This assurance which Joshua here gives them was so well grounded that it would enable one Israelite to chase a thousand Canaanites, and two to put ten thousand to flight; and it would be abundantly strengthened by remembering the song of Moses, dictated forty years before, which plainly foretold the dividing of Jordan and the influence it would have upon the driving out of the Canaanites. <reference osisRef="Exod.15.15-Exod.15.17">Exod. xv. 15-17</reference>, "<hi type="italic">The inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away,</hi> and so be effectually driven out; they shall be as still as a stone till thy people pass over, and then thou shalt bring them in and plant them." Note, God's glorious appearances for his church and people ought to be improved by us for the encouragement of our faith and hope for the future. <hi type="italic">As for God, his work is perfect.</hi> If Jordan's flood cannot keep them out, Canaan's force cannot turn them out again. <div eID="gen4143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4144" type="x-p"/> 5. He directs them to get twelve men ready, one of each tribe, who must be within call to receive such orders as Joshua should afterwards give them, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.12">v. 12</reference>. It does not appear that they were to attend the priests, and walk with them when they carried the ark, that they might more immediately be witnesses of the wonders done by it, as some think; but they were to be at hand for the service they were called to, <reference osisRef="Josh.4.4">ch. iv. 4</reference>, &c.
entries.b3f68b2fddb79b242e80edc0f2c29a1960cec13e: <div eID="gen4144" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Passage over the Jordan. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen4145" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And it came to pass, when the people removed from their tents, to pass over Jordan, and the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people; <hi type="super">15</hi> And as they that bare the ark were come unto Jordan, and the feet of the priests that bare the ark were dipped in the brim of the water, (for Jordan overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest,) <hi type="super">16</hi> That the waters which came down from above stood <hi type="italic">and</hi> rose up upon a heap very far from the city Adam, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> beside Zaretan: and those that came down toward the sea of the plain, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the salt sea, failed, <hi type="italic">and</hi> were cut off: and the people passed over right against Jericho. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the priests that bare the ark of the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan, and all the Israelites passed over on dry ground, until all the people were passed clean over Jordan. <div eID="gen4145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4146" type="x-p"/> Here we have a short and plain account of the dividing of the river Jordan, and the passage of the children of Israel through it. The story is not garnished with the flowers of rhetoric (gold needs not to be painted), but it tell us, in short, matter of fact. <div eID="gen4146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4147" type="x-p"/> I. That this river was now broader and deeper than usually it was at other times of the year, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.15">v. 15</reference>. The melting of the snow on the mountains of Lebanon, near which this river had its rise, was the occasion that at the time of harvest, barley-harvest, which was the spring of the year, Jordan overflowed all his banks. This great flood, just at that time (which Providence might have restrained for once, of which he might have ordered them to cross at another time of the year) very much magnified the power of God and his kindness to Israel. Note, Though the opposition given to the salvation of God's people have all imaginable advantages, yet God can and will conquer it. Let the banks of Jordan be filled to the brink, filled till they run over, it is as easy to Omnipotence to divide them, and dry them up, as if they were ever so narrow, ever so shallow; it is all one with the Lord. <div eID="gen4147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4148" type="x-p"/> II. That as soon as ever the feet of the priests dipped in the brim of the water the stream stopped immediately, as if a sluice had been led down to dam it up, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.15-Josh.3.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. So that the waters above swelled, stood on a heap, and ran back, and yet, as it should seem did not spread, but congealed, which unaccountable rising of the river was observed with amazement by those that live upward upon it many miles off, and the remembrance of it remained among them long after: the waters on the other side this invisible dam ran down of course, and left the bottom of the river dry as far downward, it is likely, as they swelled upward. When they passed through the red Sea, the waters were a wall on either hand, here only on the right-hand. Note, The God of nature can, when he pleases, change the course of nature, and alter its properties, can turn fluids into solids, <hi type="italic">waters into standing rocks,</hi> as, on the contrary, <hi type="italic">rocks into standing waters,</hi> to serve his own purposes. See <reference osisRef="Ps.114.5">Ps. cxiv. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.8">8</reference>. What cannot God do? What will he not do for the perfecting of his peoples, salvation? Sometimes he <hi type="italic">cleaves the earth with rivers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.9">Hab. iii. 9</reference>), and sometimes, as here, cleaves the rivers without earth. It is easy to imagine how, when the course of this strong rapid stream was arrested on a sudden, <hi type="italic">the waters roared and were troubled,</hi> so that the mountains seemed to <hi type="italic">shake with the swelling thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.3">Ps. xlvi. 3</reference>), how <hi type="italic">the floods lifted up their voice, the floods lifted up their waves,</hi> while the Lord on high showed himself <hi type="italic">mightier than the noise of</hi> these <hi type="italic">many waters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4">Ps. xciii. 3, 4</reference>. With reference to this the prophet asks, <hi type="italic">Was the Lord displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers?</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.8">Hab. iii. 8</reference>. No, <hi type="italic">Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.3.13">v. 13</reference>. In allusion to this, it is foretold, among the great things God will do for the gospel church in the latter days, that the great river Euphrates shall be dried up, that <hi type="italic">the way of the kings of the east may be prepared,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.16.12">Rev. xvi. 12</reference>. When the time has come for Israel's entrance into the land of promise all difficulties shall be conquered, <hi type="italic">mountains shall become plains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.7">Zech. iv. 7</reference>) and rivers become dry, for the <hi type="italic">ransomed of the Lord to pass over.</hi> When we have finished our pilgrimage through this wilderness, death will be like this Jordan between us and the heavenly Canaan, but the ark of the covenant has prepare us a way through it; it is the last enemy that shall be destroyed. <div eID="gen4148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4149" type="x-p"/> III. That <hi type="italic">the people passed over right against Jericho,</hi> which was, 1. An instance of their boldness, and a noble defiance of their enemies. Jericho was one of the strongest cities, and yet they dared to face it at their first entrance. 2. It was an encouragement to them to venture through Jordan, for Jericho was a goodly city and the country about it extremely pleasant; and, having that in view as their own, what difficulties could discourage them from taking possession? 3. It would increase the confusion and terror of their enemies, who no doubt strictly observed their motions, and were the amazed spectators of this work of wonders. <div eID="gen4149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4150" type="x-p"/> IV. That the priests <hi type="italic">stood still in the midst of Jordan while all the people passed over,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.3.17">v. 17</reference>. There the ark was appointed to be, to show that the same power that parted the waters kept them parted as long as there was occasion; and had not the divine presence, of which the ark was a token, been their security, the waters would have returned upon them and buried them. There the priests were appointed to stand still, 1. To try their faith, whether they could venture to take their post, when god assigned it to them, with mountains of water over their heads. As they made a bold step when they set the first foot into Jordan, so now they made a bold stand when they tarried longest in Jordan; but they knew they carried their own protection with them. Note, Ministers in times of peril should be examples of courage and confidence in the divine goodness. 2. It was to encourage the faith of the people, that they might go triumphantly into Canaan, and <hi type="italic">fear no evil,</hi> no, not in this <hi type="italic">valley of the shadow of death</hi> (for so the divided river was), being assured of God's presence, which interposed between them and the greatest danger, between them and the proud waters, which otherwise had gone over their souls. Thus in the greatest dangers the saints are <hi type="italic">comforted</hi> with <hi type="italic">his rod and his staff,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Ps. xxiii. 4</reference>.  <chapter eID="Josh.3"/> <div eID="gen4150" type="x-p"/>

entries.f6ef9e90c185d48632ecb557119de3d81511d7b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1983"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.3.1-Josh.3.6">Jos 3:1-6</reference>. Joshua Comes to Jordan.</title> <div sID="gen2638" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1983"/><hi type="bold">1. Joshua rose early in the morning--</hi>On the day following that on which the spies had returned with their encouraging report. The camp was broken up in "Shittim" (the acacia groves), and removed to the eastern bank of the Jordan. The duration of their stay is indicated (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.2">Jos 3:2</reference>), being, according to Hebrew reckoning, only one entire day, including the evening of arrival and the morning of the passage; and such a time would be absolutely necessary for so motley an assemblage of men, women, and children, with all their gear and cattle to make ready for going into an enemy's country. <div eID="gen2638" type="x-p"/>
entries.301fbf7d7bce3cb803540ddd5d08c3b0c5ab0656: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1984"/><div sID="gen2639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1984"/><hi type="bold">2-4. the officers went through the host; And they commanded the people--</hi>The instructions given at this time and in this place were different from those described (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.11">Jos 1:11</reference>). <div eID="gen2639" type="x-p"/>
entries.ba5151e1c6e16efa4163b7f2cca723026a28c66c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1986"/><div sID="gen2642" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1986"/><hi type="bold">5. Joshua said unto the people--</hi>rather "had said," for as he speaks of "to-morrow," the address must have been made previous to the day of crossing, and the sanctification was in all probability the same as Moses had commanded before the giving of the law, consisting of an outward cleansing (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.10-Exod.19.15">Ex 19:10-15</reference>) preparatory to that serious and devout state of mind with which so great a manifestation should be witnessed. <div eID="gen2642" type="x-p"/>
entries.308d662d6c7baa646b210d2f5e4bb8348534598a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1987"/><div sID="gen2643" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1987"/><hi type="bold">6. Joshua spake unto the priests--</hi>This order to the priests would be given privately, and involving as it did an important change in the established order of march, it must be considered as announced in the name and by the authority of God. Moreover, as soon as the priests stepped into the waters of Jordan, they were to stand still. The ark was to accomplish what had been done by the rod of Moses.<div eID="gen2643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2644" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Josh.3.7">Jos 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.8">8</reference>. The Lord Encourages Joshua. <div eID="gen2644" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b9c9a3051e5588e85ad8456352ab1b20d94dfef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1988"/><div sID="gen2645" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1988"/><hi type="bold">7-8. the Lord said to Joshua, This day will I ... magnify thee in the sight of all Israel--</hi>Joshua had already received distinguished honors (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.13">Ex 24:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.31.7">De 31:7</reference>). But a higher token of the divine favor was now to be publicly bestowed on him, and evidence given in the same unmistakable manner that his mission and authority were from God as was that of Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.31">Ex 14:31</reference>). <div eID="gen2645" type="x-p"/>
entries.90164b7d4fa458b7ee61afbfe2658517eee52469: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1989"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.3.9-Josh.3.13">Jos 3:9-13</reference>. Joshua Encourages the People.</title> <div sID="gen2646" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1989"/><hi type="bold">9-13. Come hither, and hear the words of the Lord--</hi>It seems that the Israelites had no intimation how they were to cross the river till shortly before the event. The premonitory address of Joshua, taken in connection with the miraculous result exactly as he had described it, would tend to increase and confirm their faith in the God of their fathers as not a dull, senseless, inanimate thing like the idols of the nations, but a Being of life, power, and activity to defend them and work for them. <div eID="gen2646" type="x-p"/>
entries.25ed2ec244a55a5f1b8f141252d7f2cf8bb06dab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1990"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.3.14-Josh.3.17">Jos 3:14-17</reference>. The Waters of Jordan Are Divided.</title> <div sID="gen2647" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1990"/><hi type="bold">14-16. And it came to pass, when the people removed from their tents, &c.--</hi>To understand the scene described we must imagine the band of priests with the ark on their shoulders, standing on the depressed edge of the river, while the mass of the people were at a mile's distance. Suddenly the whole bed of the river was dried up; a spectacle the more extraordinary in that it took place in the time of harvest, corresponding to our April or May--when "the Jordan overfloweth all its banks." The original words may be more properly rendered "fills all its banks." Its channel, snow-fed from Lebanon, was at its greatest height--brimful; a translation which gives the only true description of the state of Jordan in harvest as observed by modern travellers. The river about Jericho is, in ordinary appearance, about fifty or sixty yards in breadth. But as seen in harvest, it is twice as broad; and in ancient times, when the hills on the right and left were much more drenched with rain and snow than since the forests have disappeared, the river must, from a greater accession of water, have been broader still than at harvest-time in the present day. <div eID="gen2647" type="x-p"/>
entries.8cf28296678e1d5b793cd710818dcd48a6f261d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1992"/><div sID="gen2654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1992"/><hi type="bold">17. the priests ... and all the Israelites passed over on dry ground--</hi>the river about Jericho has a firm pebbly bottom, on which the host might pass, without inconvenience when the water was cleared off. <chapter eID="Josh.3"/>

entries.4573e95980d5927fbf0fb79ca1d737f2b82c99b8: <div eID="gen7443" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen7444" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7445" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7445" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7444" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7446" type="x-p"/> The Israelitish camp removes from Shittim to Jordan, <reference osisRef="Jos.3.1">Jos 3:1</reference>. The officers inform them how they are to pass the river, and the distance they are to keep from the ark, <reference osisRef="Jos.3.2-Jos.3.4">Jos 3:2-4</reference>. Joshua directs the people, <reference osisRef="Jos.3.5">Jos 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.3.6">Jos 3:6</reference>; and the Lord gives directions to Joshua, <reference osisRef="Jos.3.7">Jos 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.3.8">Jos 3:8</reference>. He delivers the Lord's message to the people, and foretells the miraculous passage and division of Jordan, <reference osisRef="Jos.3.9-Jos.3.13">Jos 3:9-13</reference>. The priests, bearing the ark, enter the river, and immediately the waters are cut off, and the priests stand on dry ground, in the bed of the river, till all the camp passes over, <reference osisRef="Jos.3.14-Jos.3.17">Jos 3:14-17</reference>. <div eID="gen7446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7447" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen7447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7448" type="x-p"/> Joshua rose early - Archbishop Usher supposes that this was upon Wednesday, the 28th of April, A. M. 2553, the fortieth year after the exodus from Egypt. From Shittim, where they had lately been encamped, to Jordan, was about sixty stadia, according to Josephus; that is, about eight English miles.
entries.d7161f070ac55428c161672b53c750ab30ed0c4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen7448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7449" type="x-p"/> After three days - These three days are probably to be thus understood: As soon as Joshua took the command of the army, he sent the spies to ascertain the state of Jericho; as we have seen <reference osisRef="Jos.1.12">Jos 1:12</reference>. They returned at the end of three days, or rather on the third day, and made their report. It was at this time, immediately on the return of the spies, that he made the proclamation mentioned here; in consequence of which the people immediately struck their tents, and marched forward to Jordan.
entries.d66953c2c1a3c5c3ccb0d6d6628f0ef75d195916: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen7449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7450" type="x-p"/> About two thousand cubits - This distance they were to keep, <div eID="gen7450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7451" type="x-p"/> 1. For the greater respect, because the presence of the ark was the symbol and pledge of the Divine presence. <div eID="gen7451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7452" type="x-p"/> 2. That the ark, which was to be their pilot over these waters, might be the more conspicuous which it could not have been had the people crowded upon it.
entries.7c1f93dd7f228fd1a156172214ba2888ed6b9aa0: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen7452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7453" type="x-p"/> Sanctify yourselves - What was implied in this command we are not informed; but it is likely that it was the same as that given by Moses, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.10-Exo.19.14">Exo 19:10-14</reference>. They were to wash themselves and their garments, and abstain from every thing that might indispose their minds from a profitable attention to the miracle about to be wrought in their behalf.
entries.6afa9b024c0c0fe1b469c1957cc0b3b2b416f938: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen7453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7454" type="x-p"/> Spake unto the priests, saying, Take up the ark - It is remarkable that the priests, not the Levites, whose ordinary business it was were employed to carry the ark on this occasion. Calmet conjectures that this was because it was probably carried without being wrapped up in its curtains, as it always was when the Levites carried it. Though it was the business of the Levites, the sons of Kohath, to carry the ark; yet on certain occasions the priests alone performed this office. <div eID="gen7454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7455" type="x-p"/> 1. In the present case. <div eID="gen7455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7456" type="x-p"/> 2. When they encompassed Jericho, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.6">Jos 6:6</reference>. <div eID="gen7456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7457" type="x-p"/> 3. When it was carried to the war against the Philistines by the priests, the sons of Eli, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.25">2Sam 15:25</reference>. <div eID="gen7457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7458" type="x-p"/> 4. When David sent it back to Jerusalem, at the time he was obliged to fly from it, through the rebellion of his son Absalom, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.25">2Sam 15:25</reference>; and, <div eID="gen7458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7459" type="x-p"/> 5. At the time that it was taken out of the tabernacle, to be deposited in the temple; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.6-1Kgs.8.11">1Kgs 8:6-11</reference>. <div eID="gen7459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7460" type="x-p"/> These were the most solemn occasions, and on such alone, we may presume, the priests performed this office instead of the Levites. In all their former marches the ark was carried in the center of this immense camp; (see the scheme at the end of <reference osisRef="Num.2.2">Num 2:2</reference> (note) of the book of Numbers); but now it was to proceed at the head of the army, and to go before them, and at such a distance, about three quarters of a mile, that the whole camp might see it as their guide.
entries.586715ca0806153550310bb7cbde6b6902f9c3a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen7460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7461" type="x-p"/> This day will I begin to magnify thee - By making him the instrument in this miraculous passage, he did him honor and gave him high credit in the sight of the people: hence his authority was established, and obedience to him as their leader fully secured. What must have confirmed this authority was, his circumstantially foretelling how the waters should be cut off as soon as the feet of the priests had touched them, <reference osisRef="Jos.3.13">Jos 3:13</reference>. This demonstrated that the secret of the Lord was with him.
entries.457a1913be2176640adf049a20444521d53b2683: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen7461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7462" type="x-p"/> Ye shall stand still in Jordan - The priests proceeded first with the ark, and entered into the bed of the river the course of which was immediately arrested, the waters collecting above the place where the priests stood, while the stream fell off towards the Dead Sea; so that the whole channel below where the priests were standing became dry. The whole camp, therefore, passed over below where the priests were standing, keeping at the distance of two thousand cubits from the ark; this they would readily do, as the whole bed of the river was dry for many miles below the place where the priests entered.
entries.b32262da90647c65474f15b6dc75150fed74a190: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen7462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7463" type="x-p"/> Hereby ye shall know that the living God is among you - The Israelites were apt to be discouraged, and to faint at even the appearance of danger; it was necessary, therefore, that they should have the fullest assurance of the presence and assistance of God in the important enterprise on which they were now entering. They are to combat idolaters, who have nothing to trust in and help them but gods of wood, stone, and metal: whereas they are to have the living God in the midst of them - He who is the author of life and of being - who can give, or take it away, at his pleasure; and who by this miracle proved that he had undertaken to guide and defend them: and Joshua makes this manifestation of God the proof that he will drive out the Hittites, Hivites, etc, before them. With regard to the situation of each of these nations in the land of Canaan, Calmet remarks, that those called Canaanites chiefly inhabited what is called Phoenicia, the environs of Tyre and Sidon: the Hittites occupied the mountains, southward of the promised land: the Hivites dwelt by Ebal and Gerizim, Sichem and Gibeon, towards the mountains of Hermon: the Perizzites were probably not a distinct nation or tribe, but rather villagers, scattered through the country in general: the Girgashites possessed the country beyond the Jordan, towards the lake of Gennesareth: the Jebusites possessed Jerusalem: and the Amorites occupied the mountainous country in the vicinity of the western part of the Dead Sea, and also that part of the land of Moab which the Israelites conquered from Sihon and Og.
entries.18522bd67e4ce81960eeb8b157d40ce0c9805ce0: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen7463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7464" type="x-p"/> Take you twelve men - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.4.2">Jos 4:2</reference>.
entries.e9ef8860176d879b82a69f59e6bf540706a402a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen7464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7465" type="x-p"/> And the feet of the priests - were dipped in the brim of the water - Thus we find that every thing occurred exactly in the way in which Joshua had foretold it. This must have greatly increased his credit among the people. <div eID="gen7465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7466" type="x-p"/> For Jordan overfloweth all his banks, etc. - It has often been remarked that there was no need of a miracle in crossing Jordan, as it is but an inconsiderable stream, easily fordable, being but about twenty yards in breadth. But the circumstance marked here by the sacred historian proves that there was a time in the year, viz., in the harvest, that this said river overflowed its banks; and this is confirmed by another place in Scripture, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.15">1Chr 12:15</reference>. As the miracle reported here took place about the beginning of April, a time in which rivers in general are less than in winter, it may be asked how there could be such an increase of waters at this time? The simple fact is, that the Jordan, as we have already seen, has its origin at the foot of Mount Lebanon, which mountain is always covered with snow during the winter months; in those months therefore the river is low: but when the summer's sun has melted these snows, there is consequently a prodigious increase of waters, so that the old channel is not capable of containing them; this accounts for the statement in the text that the Jordan overfloweth his banks all the time of harvest; and this was the time which God chose they should pass over it, that a miraculous interposition might be necessary, and that by the miracle they should be convinced of his omnipotence, who was not only their guide, but had promised to put them in possession of this good land.
entries.dd6bc59bb13defe4e1daddcc64ec8d50ee54a2d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen7466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7467" type="x-p"/> Rose up upon a heap - That is, they continued to accumulate, filling up the whole of the channel toward the source, and the adjacent ground over which they were now spread, to a much greater depth, the power of God giving a contrary direction to the current. We need not suppose them to be gathered up like a mountain, instar montis, as the Vulgate expresses it, but that they continued to flow back in the course of the channel; and ere they could have reached the lake of Gennesareth, where they might have been easily accumulated, the whole Israelitish army would have all got safely to the opposite side. <div eID="gen7467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7468" type="x-p"/> Very far from the city Adam - beside Zaretan - Where these places were it is difficult to say. The city Adam is wholly unknown. From <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.12">1Kgs 4:12</reference> we learn that Zartanah was below Jezreel near Bethshean, or Scythopolis, and not far from Succoth, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.46">1Kgs 7:46</reference>. And it appears from <reference osisRef="Gen.33.17">Gen 33:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.27">Jos 13:27</reference>, that Succoth lay on the east side of Jordan, not far from the lake of Gennesareth; and probably Adam was on the same side to the north of Succoth. It is probable that the Israelites crossed the Jordan near Bethabara, where John baptized, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.28">Joh 1:28</reference>, and which probably had its name, the house of passage, from this very circumstance. After all, it is extremely difficult to ascertain the exact situation of these places, as in the lapse of upwards of 3,000 years the face of the country must have been materially changed. Seas, rivers, and mountains, change not; and though we cannot ascertain the spot, it is sufficiently evident that we can come near to the place. It has been considered a lame objection against the truth of the Iliad that the situation of Troy cannot now be exactly ascertained. There are even many ancient cities and considerable towns in Europe, that, though they still bear their former names, do not occupy the same spot. There are not a few of those even in England; among such Norwich, Salisbury, etc., may be ranked, neither of which is in its primitive situation. <div eID="gen7468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7469" type="x-p"/> Right against Jericho - It would be impossible for the whole camp to pass over in the space opposite to Jericho, as they must have taken up some miles in breadth, besides the 2,000 cubits which were left on the right between them and the ark; but the river was divided opposite to Jericho, and there the camp began to pass over.
entries.f7f455a329ce85df18bc1cb75dd7924442e59c2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen7469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7470" type="x-p"/> The priests - stood firm on dry ground - They stood in the mid channel, and shifted not their position till the camp, consisting of nearly 600,000 effective men, besides women, children, etc., had passed over. <div eID="gen7470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7471" type="x-p"/> 1. Is it not surprising that the Canaanites did not dispute this passage with the Israelites? It is likely they would, had they had any expectation that such a passage would have been attempted. They must have known that the Israelitish camp was on the other side of the Jordan, but could they have supposed that a passage for such a host was possible when the banks of the Jordan were quite overflowed? It was not merely because they were panic struck that they did not dispute this passage, but because they must have supposed it impossible; and when they found the attempt was made, the passage was effected before they could prepare to prevent it. <div eID="gen7471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7472" type="x-p"/> 2. God now appears in such a way, and works in such a manner, as to leave no doubt concerning his presence or his power, or of his love to Israel. After this, was it possible for this people ever to doubt his being or his bounty? This, with the miraculous passage of the Red Sea, were well calculated to have established their faith for ever; and those who did not yield to the evidence afforded by these two miracles were incapable of rational conviction. <div eID="gen7472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7473" type="x-p"/> 3. In some respects the passage of the Jordan was more strikingly miraculous than that even of the Red Sea. In the latter God was pleased to employ an agent; the sea went back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, <reference osisRef="Exo.14.21">Exo 14:21</reference>. Nothing of this kind appeared in the passage of the Jordan; a very rapid river (for so all travelers allow it to be) went back to its source without any kind of agency but the invisible hand of the invisible God. <div eID="gen7473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7474" type="x-p"/> 4. Through the whole period of the Jewish history these miracles, so circumstantially related, were never denied by any, but on the contrary conscientiously believed by all. Nor did any of them in their revolts from God, which were both foul and frequent, ever call these great facts in question, when even so full of enmity against God as to blaspheme his name, and give his glory to dumb idols! Is not this a manifest proof that these facts were incontestable? and that Jehovah had so done his marvellous works that they should be had in everlasting remembrance? Reader, the same God who is over all is rich in mercy to all that call upon him. He changes not, neither is he weary: trust in the Lord for ever, for in the Lord Jehovah is everlasting strength; and He ever saves his followers out of the hands of all their enemies, and, having guided them by his counsel, will receive them into his glory.  <chapter eID="Josh.3"/> <div eID="gen7474" type="x-p"/>

entries.a9e59ce2232292c4ced293cc059455796a484cc3: <reference osisRef="Josh.3.1-Josh.3.4">Jos 3:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen2688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2689" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Arrangements for the Passage through the Jordan</hi>. - When they reached the Jordan, the Israelites rested till they passed over. לוּן, <hi type="italic">to pass the night</hi>; then in a wider sense to tarry, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.31">Pro 15:31</reference>; here it means to rest. According to <reference osisRef="Josh.3.2">Jos 3:2</reference>, they stayed there three days. “<hi type="italic">At the end</hi> (after the expiration) <hi type="italic">of three days</hi>” cannot refer to the three days mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.1.11">Jos 1:11</reference>, if only because of the omission of the article, apart from the reasons given in the note upon <reference osisRef="Josh.1.11">Jos 1:11</reference>, which preclude the supposition that the two are identical. The reasons why the Israelites stayed three days by the side of the Jordan, after leaving Shittim, are not given, but they are not difficult to guess; for, in the first place, before it could be possible to pass into an enemy’s country, not only with an army, but with all the people, including wives, children, and all their possessions, and especially when the river had first of all to be crossed, it must have been necessary to make many preparations, which would easily occupy two or three days. Besides this, the Jordan at that time was so high as to overflow its banks, so that it was impossible to cross the fords, and they were obliged to wait till this obstruction was removed. But as soon as Joshua was assured that the Lord would make a way for His people, he issued the following instructions through the proper officers to all the people in the camp: “<hi type="italic">When ye see the</hi> <hi type="italic">ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, and </hi>(<hi type="italic">see</hi>)<hi type="italic">the Levitical priests bear it, then ye shall remove from your place, and go after it: yet there shall be a space between you and it, about two thousand cubits by measure: come not near unto it; that ye may know the way by which ye must go: for ye have not passed this way yesterday and the day before</hi>.” On the expression “the Levitical priests,” see at <reference osisRef="Deut.31.25">Deu 31:25</reference>, as compared with <reference osisRef="Josh.3.9">Jos 3:9</reference> and Jos 17:9. בּינו, both here and in <reference osisRef="Josh.8.11">Jos 8:11</reference>, should probably be pointed בּינו (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §266, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.). This command referred simply to the march from the last resting-place by the Jordan into the river itself, and not to the passage through the river, during which the priests remained standing with the ark in the bed of the river until the people had all passed through (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.8">Jos 3:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.3.17">Jos 3:17</reference>).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> maintains that this statement, according to which the Israelites were more than 2000 cubits from the place of crossing, is not in harmony with <reference osisRef="Josh.3.1">Jos 3:1</reference>, where they are said to have been by the Jordan already; but he can only show this supposed discrepancy in the text by so pressing the expression, they “came to Jordan,” as to make it mean that the whole nation was encamped so close to the edge of the river, that at the very first step the people took their feet would touch the water.</note> <div eID="gen2689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2690" type="x-p"/> The people were to keep about 2000 cubits away from the ark. This was not done, however, to prevent their going wrong in the unknown way, and so missing the ford, for that was impossible under the circumstances; but the ark was carried in front of the people, not so much to show the road as to make a road by dividing the waters of the Jordan, and the people were to keep at a distance from it, that they might not lose sight of the ark, but keep their eyes fixed upon it, and know the road by looking at the ark of the covenant by which the road had been made, i.e., might know and observe how the Lord, through the medium of the ark, was leading them to Canaan by a way which they had never traversed before, i.e., by a miraculous way.
entries.f412e593b2e71b23b0317222f2185a46aad927c7: <reference osisRef="Josh.3.5-Josh.3.6">Jos 3:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen2690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2691" type="x-p"/> Joshua then issued instructions (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) to the people to sanctify themselves, because on the morrow the Lord would do wonders among them; and (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) to the priests, to carry the ark of the covenant in front of the people. The issuing of these commands with the prediction of the miracle presupposes that the Lord had already made known His will to Joshua, and serves to confirm our conclusions as to the arrangement of the materials. The sanctification of the people did not consist in the washing of their clothes, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Exod.19.10">Exo 19:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.14">Exo 19:14</reference>, in connection with the act of sanctification, for there was no time for this; nor did it consist in merely changing their clothes, which might be a substitute for washing, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.35.2">Gen 35:2</reference>, or in abstinence from connubial intercourse (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.15">Exo 19:15</reference>), for this was only the outward side of sanctification. It consisted in spiritual purification also, i.e., in turning the heart to God, in faith and trust in His promise, and in willing obedience to His commandments, that they should lay to heart in a proper way the miracle of grace which the Lord was about to work in the midst of them and on their behalf on the following day. “<hi type="italic">Wonders</hi>:” those miraculous displays of the omnipotence of God for the realization of His covenant of grace, which He had already promised in connection with the conquest of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.10">Exo 34:10</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Josh.3.6">Jos 3:6</reference>, where the command to the priests is given, the fulfilment of the command is also mentioned, and the course of events anticipated in consequence.
entries.5d66a1cfe5d7d1c1003c7b817d1fd69ae04ad7ae: <reference osisRef="Josh.3.7-Josh.3.8">Jos 3:7-8</reference> <hi type="italic">Commencement of the Crossing</hi>. - First of all (in <reference osisRef="Josh.3.7">Jos 3:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.3.8">Jos 3:8</reference>), the revelation made by God to Joshua, that He would begin this day to make him great, i.e., to glorify him before the Israelites, and the command to the priests who bore the ark of the covenant to stand still in the river, when they came to the water of the Jordan; then (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.9-Josh.3.13">Jos 3:9-13</reference>) the publication of this promise and command to the people; and lastly (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.14-Josh.3.17">Jos 3:14-17</reference>), the carrying out of the command. אחל, I will <hi type="italic">begin</hi> to make thee great. The miraculous guidance of the people through the Jordan was only the beginning of the whole series of miracles by which the Lord put His people in possession of the promised land, and glorifies Joshua in the sight of Israel in the fulfilment of his office, as He had glorified Moses before. Just as Moses was accredited in the sight of the people, as the servant of the Lord in whom they could trust, by the miraculous division of the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.31">Exo 14:31</reference>), so Joshua was accredited as the leader of Israel, whom the Almighty God acknowledged as He had His servant Moses, by the similar miracle, the division of the waters of Jordan. Only the most important points in the command of God to the priests are given in v. 8. The command itself is communicated more fully afterwards in the address to the people, in v. 13. When they came with the ark to the end of the waters of Jordan-i.e., not to the opposite side, but to the nearest bank; that is to say, as soon as they reached the water in the bed of the river-they were to stand still (vid., v. 15, and <reference osisRef="Josh.4.11">Jos 4:11</reference>), in order, as we see from what follows, to form a dam as it were against the force of the water, which was miraculously arrested in its course, and piled up in a heap. Moses divided the waters of the Red Sea with his <hi type="italic">rod</hi>; Joshua was to do the same to the Jordan with the <hi type="italic">ark of the covenant</hi>, the appointed symbol and vehicle of the presence of the Almighty God since the conclusion of the covenant. Wherever the ordinary means of grace are at hand, God attaches the operations of His grace to them; for He is a God of order, who does not act in an arbitrary manner in the selection of His means.
entries.b08e590957c2fee496d002c9027b4c0b4599da52: <reference osisRef="Josh.3.9-Josh.3.10">Jos 3:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen2691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2692" type="x-p"/> The summons to the children of Israel, i.e., to the whole nation in the persons of its representatives, to draw near (גּשׁוּ for גּשׁוּ, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.38">1Sa 14:38</reference>; Rth 2:14) to hear the words of the Lord its God, points to the importance of the following announcement by which Israel was to learn that there was a living God in the midst of it, who had the power to fulfil His word. Jehovah is called a “living God,” in contrast with the dead gods of the heathen, as a God who proved himself to be living, with special reference to those “divine operations by which God had shown that He was living and watchful on behalf of His people; just as His <hi type="italic">being in the midst</hi> of the people did not denote a naked presence, but a striking degree of presence on the part of God in relation to the performance of extraordinary operations, or the manifestation of peculiar care” (<hi type="italic">Seb. Schmidt</hi>). The God of Israel would now manifest himself as a living God by the extermination of the Canaanites, seven tribes of whom are enumerated, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference> (see the remarks on this passage). Joshua mentions the destruction of these nations as the purpose which God had in view in the miraculous guidance of Israel through the Jordan, to fill the Israelites with confidence for their entrance into the promised land.<note placement="foot">“He extends the force of the miracle beyond their entrance into the land, and properly so, since the mere opening of a way into a hostile country from which there would be no retreat, would be nothing but exposure to death. For they would either easily fall, through being entangled in difficulties and in an unknown region, or they would perish through want. Joshua therefore foretold, that when God drove back the river it would be as if He had stretched out His hand to strike all the inhabitants of the land, and that the proof which He gave of His power in their crossing the Jordan would be a certain presage of victory, to be gained over all the tribes.”</note>
entries.abe942d6f313bf3f17b8300ef489f1dcd3f091a1: <reference osisRef="Josh.3.11">Jos 3:11</reference> <div eID="gen2692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2693" type="x-p"/> After this inspiriting promise, Joshua informed the people what the Lord intended to do first: “<hi type="italic">Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of the whole earth will go before you</hi> <hi type="italic">into Jordan</hi>.” כּל־הארץ 'adown is a genitive dependent upon הברית ארון, the strict subordination of the construct state being loosened in this case by the article before the <hi type="italic">nomen regens</hi>. The punctuators have therefore separated it from the latter by <hi type="italic">sakeph - katon</hi>, without thereby explaining it as in opposition or giving any support to the mistaken exposition of <hi type="italic">Buxtorff</hi> and <hi type="italic">Drusius</hi>, that “the ark of the covenant is called the ruler of the whole earth.” The description of Jehovah as “Lord of the whole earth,” which is repeated in <reference osisRef="Josh.3.13">Jos 3:13</reference>, is very appropriately chosen for the purpose of strengthening confidence in the omnipotence of the Lord. This epithet “exalted the government of God over all the elements of the world, that the Israelites might have no doubt that as seas and rivers are under His control, the waters, although liquid by nature, would become stable at His nod” (<hi type="italic">Calvin</hi>). The expression, “<hi type="italic">passeth over before you into</hi> <hi type="italic">Jordan</hi>,” is more precisely explained in the course of the narrative: the ark of the covenant went (was carried) before the people into the river, and then stood still, as the bulwark of the people, till the passage was completed; so that the word “before” indicates the protection which it would afford.
entries.b14762fd20ae11cdb270fc1d33b56d0932ab1446: <reference osisRef="Josh.3.12-Josh.3.13">Jos 3:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen2693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2694" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And take to you</hi> (i.e., appoint) <hi type="italic">twelve men out of the tribes</hi> of Israel, one for each tribe.” For what purpose is not stated here, but is apparent from what follows (Jos 4:2.). The choice or appointment of these men was necessarily commanded before the crossing commenced, as they were to stand by the side of Joshua, or near the bearers of the ark of the covenant, so as to be at hand to perform the duty to be entrusted to them (Jos 4:3.). Joshua then concludes by foretelling the miracle itself: “<hi type="italic">It will come to pass, that when the soles of the feet of the priests who bear the ark of the Lord shall settle down in the water of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off; namely, the waters flowing down from above, and shall stand still as one heap.”</hi> “<hi type="italic">Shall be cut off</hi>,” so as to disappear; namely, at the place where the priests stand with the ark of the covenant. This took place through the waters standing still as a heap, or being heaped up, at some distance above the standing-place. אחד נד is an accusative of more precise definition. The expression is taken from the song of Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.8">Exo 15:8</reference>).
entries.f2c8a58ed14a32b985e39433053ceafc87927c7e: <reference osisRef="Josh.3.14-Josh.3.16">Jos 3:14-16</reference> <div eID="gen2694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2695" type="x-p"/> The event corresponded to the announcement. - <reference osisRef="Josh.3.14">Jos 3:14</reference>-16. When the people left their tents to go over the Jordan, and the priests, going before the ark of the covenant, dipped their feet in the water (“the brim of the water,” <reference osisRef="Josh.3.15">Jos 3:15</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.3.8">Jos 3:8</reference>), although the Jordan was filled over all its banks throughout the whole time of harvest, the waters stood still: the waters flowing down from above stood as a heap at a very great distance off, by the town of Adam, on the side of Zarthan; and the waters flowing down to the salt sea were entirely cut off, so that the people went through the dried bed of the river opposite to Jericho. <reference osisRef="Josh.3.14-Josh.3.16">Jos 3:14-16</reference> form one large period, consisting of three protases (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.14">Jos 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.15">Jos 3:15</reference>), the first and third of which are each of them more precisely defined by a circumstantial clause, and also of three apodoses (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.16">Jos 3:16</reference>). In the protases the construction passes from the infinitive (בּנסע and כּבוא) into the finite verb (נטבּלוּ), - a thing of frequent occurrence (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §350). The circumstantial clause (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Josh.3.15">Jos 3:15</reference></hi>), “<hi type="italic">and the Jordan was</hi> <hi type="italic">filled over all its banks all the days of harvest</hi>,” brings out in all its fulness the miracle of the stoppage of the water by the omnipotence of God. Every attempt to explain the miracle as a natural occurrence is thereby prevented; so that Eichhorn pronounces the clause a gloss, and endeavours in this manner to get rid of it altogether. על־כּל־גּבותיו might mean full against all its banks, flowing with its banks full, or “full to the brim” (<hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, Pal. ii. p. 262, according to the lxx and <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>.); but if we compare <reference osisRef="Josh.4.18">Jos 4:18</reference>, “the waters of Jordan returned to their place, and went over all its banks as before,” with the parallel passage in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Isa 8:7</reference>, “the river comes up over all its channels and goes over all its banks,” there can be no doubt that the words refer to an overflowing of the banks, and not merely to their being filled to the brim, so that the words must be rendered “go over the banks.” But we must not therefore understand them as meaning that the whole of the Ghor was flooded. The Jordan flows through the Ghor, which is two hours’ journey broad at Beisan, and even broader to the south of that (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.1.1">Deu 1:1</reference>), in a valley about a quarter of an hour in breadth which lies forty or fifty feet lower, and, being covered with trees and reeds, presents a striking contrast to the sandy slopes which bound it on both sides. In many places this strip of vegetation occupies a still deeper portion of the lower valley, which is enclosed by shallow banks not more than two or three feet high, so that, strictly speaking, we might distinguish three different banks at the places referred to: namely, the upper or outer banks, which form the first slope of the great valley; the lower or middle banks, embracing that strip of land which is covered with vegetation; and then the true banks of the river’s bed (see <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, Syr. pp. 593ff., and <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, Pal. ii. pp. 254ff., and Bibl. Researches, pp. 333ff.). The flood never reaches beyond the lower line of the Ghor, which is covered with vegetation, but even in modern times this line has sometimes been overflowed. For example, <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> (Pal. ii. p. 255, compared with p. 263) found the river so swollen when he visited it in 1838, that it filled its bed to the very brim, and in some places flowed over and covered the ground where the bushes grew. This rise of the water still takes place at the time of harvest in April and at the beginning of May (see at Lev 23:9.), and therefore really at the close of the rainy reason, and after the snow has been long melted upon Hermon, as it is then that the lake of Tiberias reaches its greatest height, in consequence of the rainy season and the melting of the snow, so that it is only then that the Jordan flows with its full stream into the Dead Sea (<hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, ii. p. 263). At this time of the year the river cannot of course be waded through even at its shallowest fords, whereas this is possible in the summer season, when the water is low. It is only by swimming that it can possibly be crossed, and even that cannot be accomplished without great danger, as it is ten or twelve feet deep in the neighbourhood of Jericho, and the current is very strong (vid., <hi type="italic">Seetzen,</hi> R. ii. pp. 301, 320-1; <hi type="italic">Rob</hi>. ii. p. 256). Crossing at this season was regarded as a very extraordinary feat in ancient times, so that it is mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.15">1Ch 12:15</reference> as a heroic act on the part of the brave Gadites. It may possibly have been in this way that the spies crossed and recrossed the river a few days before. But that was altogether impossible for the people of Israel with their wives and children. <div eID="gen2695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2696" type="x-p"/> It was necessary, therefore, that the Lord of the whole earth should make a road by a miracle of His omnipotence, which arrested the descending waters in their course, so that they stood still as a heap “<hi type="italic">very far</hi>,” sc., from the place of crossing, “<hi type="italic">by the town of</hi> <hi type="italic">Adam”</hi> (בּאדם must not be altered into מאדם, from Adam, according to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>), “<hi type="italic">which is by the side of Zarthan</hi>.” The city of Adam, which is not mentioned anywhere else (and which <hi type="italic">Luther </hi>has erroneously understood as an appellative, according to the Arabic, “people of the city”), is not to be confounded with Adamah, in the tribe of Naphtali (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.36">Jos 19:36</reference>).
